title: Subha and the stranger
hook: a man blocks Subha's path in a mango grove, praising her eyes; she shows him what an eye is (Therigatha, Subha)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambapali walked through her own body, then and now, sacca, the truth-speaker's word. Your line was so it was, so it is. Did you meet your reflection without a verdict? Today, another nun, and a man who won't let her pass. Day seven hundred ninety-two.

A path through a mango grove, the one known as Jivaka's. A nun named Subha is walking it. A man steps into her way and stays there. What wrong have I done you, she asks, that you stand in my path? It isn't fitting for a man to touch a woman who has gone forth. He doesn't step aside. He starts talking instead: about her youth, about the forest in flower, and more than anything, about her eyes. What she says back is today's lesson.
screen: `JIVAKA'S MANGO GROVE.` → `A MAN BLOCKS THE PATH.` → `WHAT WRONG HAVE I DONE YOU?`

segments.voice: First, his pitch. In the poem he offers her a life of comfort: fine cloth, ornaments, a house, the grove in bloom and full of birdsong. Give up the robe, he says. And he keeps returning to her eyes, like a doe's, he says; nothing is dearer to him. Second, her answer. Subha takes his praise apart. What is this body you're so taken with? What is an eye? A little ball set in a hollow, she says, with a bubble in the middle and tears around it. She compares a body to a painted puppet. She has seen through what he's selling. Third, the act. Then the poem does something startling. She plucks out her eye and holds it out to him: here, take it. His desire vanishes on the spot. He asks her forgiveness, and wishes her well, and lets her go. Fourth, the ending. Subha goes on to the Buddha, and the poem says that when she saw him, her eye was restored as it had been. What to make of a story like this? Some readers hear renunciation pushed to its limit. Others hear a woman refusing to be reduced to a part of her body: he wanted the eye, so she showed him what an eye is. The poem tells it as her answer, once, not as a thing anyone is asked to repeat. And its first line still stands on its own: she names the wrong plainly, before anything else happens.
screen: `A HOUSE, CLOTH, AND HER EYES.` · `A BALL IN A HOLLOW, WITH TEARS.` · `HERE, TAKE YOUR EYE.` · `SEEING THE BUDDHA, MADE WHOLE.` · then, large: `WHAT IS AN EYE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: refuse one unwanted advance. It doesn't have to be dramatic. It might be a sales pitch, a pull from your phone, a request you keep saying yes to out of habit. Settle, and bring it to mind. Then hear Subha's first question inside: what wrong have I done, that you stand in my path? Let a no form, plain and unhurried. You don't have to say it yet. Just feel what it's like to hold it. And if someone is truly blocking your path the way the man in the grove did, that calls for more than a breath: tell someone you trust. The bell holds the time.
Cakkhu. The eye: the word behind Subha's question to a stranger who praised her eyes on a forest path, what is an eye? Today's word.
Your line: what is an eye. Today, when something is praised to sell it to you, ask Subha's question of it: what is this, really? Day seven hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Contemplating the parts of the body is a traditional Buddhist practice for loosening desire, and teachers sometimes tell Subha's story to show that practice used as a clear refusal.

fork.setup: you're Subha, walking alone in a mango grove. a man blocks your path and praises your eyes. what do you do?
options: step around him and take another path.
ask what wrong you've done, and show him what an eye is.
agree to hear him out later.
fork.reveal: she names the wrong, takes his praise apart, and in the poem holds out her own eye. his desire is gone, and he asks forgiveness.

original.note: Pali cakkhu: the eye. The stranger praises Subha's eyes; she shows him what an eye is.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gruesome story.
what it means: a nun stopped and praised for her eyes answers by showing what an eye is, and the man's desire is gone.
what a scholar hears: her name in the collection ties her to Jivaka's mango grove at Rajagaha, a place known from the suttas; her answer turns his praise into a contemplation of the body's parts.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2 (Samannaphala Sutta, set in Jivaka's mango grove at Rajagaha)

notes: All texts are paraphrased; no translation quoted.

Sensitive content: harassment and a self-inflicted wound. The script frames the eye as told once in the poem, gives two readings without ranking, and the practice adds a line to tell someone trusted if someone is truly blocking the listener's path. Keeper and owner should confirm the tone.

Confirm the paraphrase of Thig 14.1: her opening question and 'it is not fitting to touch a woman gone forth'; his offers (cloth, ornaments, house, the flowering grove); eyes like a doe's (some translations: like a kinnari's); her description of the eye (a little ball in a hollow, a bubble, tears); the painted puppet image; plucking out the eye; his remorse; her eye restored on seeing the Buddha.
Two readings ('renunciation pushed to its limit' / 'refusing to be reduced to a part of her body') are the writer's framing of modern responses.
